content.text: Claude Code's checkpoints let you rewind the files Claude edited with its own file tools in the current session. They don't cover files that only shell commands changed, most subagent edits, your own edits, symlinked or hard-linked files, or anything outside the filesystem. Use
for quick in-session undo, and keep committing to git for everything else.

A developer asks Claude Code to migrate the billing module from one date library to another. Claude edits a dozen files with its edit tool, then runs a codemod script through Bash that rewrites forty more, installs the new package, which updates the lockfile, and applies a migration to the local dev database. The tests go red. The developer presses
. The dozen edited files snap back. The forty codemod files, the lockfile and the database stay as they are. Nothing was committed before the session started, so git can't help either.
"Checkpoints can undo anything the session changed, so committing to git along the way is unnecessary." It's an understandable belief:

items.text: Rewind feels like time travel. Open the menu, pick a prompt, and the code and the conversation go back.
It's automatic. Every prompt you send creates a checkpoint, with no setup.
It lasts. Checkpoints are saved with the conversation, so
/rewind
still works after you resume a session.
The docs encourage it: rewinding makes it "low-risk to try the bolder approach first".

content.text: The half-truth: for edits Claude makes with its file tools in your main conversation, rewind is fast and reliable. But that is exactly its boundary, and most real sessions cross it.
Claude Code captures the state of your code before each prompt you send that starts a turn, and it tracks the changes made by Claude's file editing tools. Each

is saved with the conversation. Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session, and its retention sweep deletes a session's snapshots, by default about 30 days after the session last saved one. Rewinding to a checkpoint whose snapshots are gone can fail with

twice on an empty prompt, lists the prompts you sent. For each one you can restore the code and the conversation, only the conversation, or only the code, or summarize part of the conversation. The code options appear only when that checkpoint has tracked file changes to revert.
The checkpointing docs list the limits:

items.text: Files that only Bash commands changed: codemods,
npm install
, a formatter run from the shell. Once Claude has edited a file with its file tools,
/rewind
does undo later Bash changes to that file.
Edits by most
subagents
to files Claude hadn't already edited in your conversation. A forked skill running in the foreground is the exception.
Your own edits outside Claude Code and edits from other concurrent sessions, unless they touch the same files.
Symlinked and hard-linked files, which a restore skips with a
Restored the code, but skipped N files
warning. Files pnpm hard-links into place fall into this category.

content.text: Beyond files, the overview is explicit: actions that affect remote systems, such as databases, APIs and deployments, "can't be checkpointed."
Git doesn't care which program changed a file. A codemod, a package manager or your own editor all show up in

. The docs put the roles plainly: checkpoints are for "quick, session-level recovery", and git stays the tool for commits, branches and long-term history. The best-practices guide adds that they "work alongside git rather than replacing it."
A session with no way back vs one with a commit under it

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Uncommitted work in the tree, a big change, no branch
git status --short   # 14 files modified, nothing committed
claude "Migrate the billing module from moment to date-fns"

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# Branch and commit first, so git can undo anything on disk
git switch -c chore/date-fns
git add -A && git commit -m "Checkpoint before date-fns migration"
claude "Migrate src/billing/ to date-fns, run its tests, then stop."
# Review every change, whichever tool made it
git status --short && git diff --stat
# Discard it all and return to the commit (tracked and new files)
git reset --hard && git clean -fd

content.text: In the first session, the only way back is the rewind menu, and it can't restore what the codemod rewrote. In the second, the commit is a floor you can always return to.
shows the Bash-made changes the rewind menu would have missed.

blocks.title: Rewind for experiments, commit for progress

content.text: is ideal for trying the bold approach first: if it doesn't work out, restore and try the other one. Once a step passes its checks, commit it. Each commit is a rewind point that covers every file and outlives the session.

blocks.title: Neither tool can undo a side effect

content.text: A pushed branch, an applied migration or a sent email stays done: checkpoints and git both work on files. For actions like these, the docs point to your permission mode and permission rules instead.
rule makes Claude Code stop and ask you before it runs a command you can't take back:
How to apply it in your project
Before a large change, commit or stash what's in the tree and switch to a branch, so there's a clean point to return to.
Small commits after each passing step give you rewind points that cover shell commands and survive the session.
Restore Claude's edits, or just the conversation, when an approach fails. It's faster than git for that, and it can summarize a stale stretch of conversation too.

items.title: Review with git, not the rewind menu

content.text: show every change on disk, including the ones a Bash command or a subagent made. Inside the session,
gives you the same picture: its
view reads the working tree from git, while its per-turn views show only Claude's file edits.
rules on pushes, migrations and deploys. A rule matches the command text Claude writes, not every way to run the program, so it's a speed bump, not a security boundary.

items.text: Checkpoints track edits made by Claude's file tools in your session, captured before each prompt.
They miss files only Bash changed, most subagent edits, your own edits and symlinked or hard-linked files.
Remote effects such as databases, APIs and deployments can't be checkpointed at all.
Git sees every change on disk, lasts beyond the session and is shared with your team.
Use
/rewind
for quick experiments, commit at each green check, and gate irreversible commands.
